dossier.public_summary: The 14.2-day dip alternates between deep and shallow events and shows a secondary eclipse nearly half as deep as the primary, which marks it as a stellar binary at about 28 days folded at half period, not a transiting planet. Individual transits are also wildly inconsistent between sectors and between SPOC products, with some sectors showing no dip at all and a few outliers dominating the signal. Centroid is inconclusive and this pattern positively favours an eclipsing binary or blended binary as the best explanation.

reasons.why: Odd and even transits have markedly different depths, with the odd ones about 2.5 times deeper. This is the classic signature of an eclipsing binary folded at half its true period (28.4 d), not a planet at 14.2 d.

A significant secondary eclipse at ~32% of the period, nearly half as deep as the primary, indicates a stellar companion re-radiating rather than a planet. Secondary is well above any brightening artefact.

Individual transits are not consistent: three outliers dominate ~98% of the signal and two sectors show no transit. A planet on the target must be steady; this depth collapse nullifies the 14.2-d signal.

Depth really changes between sectors, even within the same pipeline product, from ~1072 ppm in sector 43 to consistent with zero in sectors 57 and 84. This is not a calibration offset but evidence the dip source is variable or blended, supporting an EB at a neighbour/alias rather than a planet on the target.
reasons.value: changes_within_a_source, p_constant_all 1.4124450428514143e-30, SPOC 2-min p_constant 3.283e-08 depth 691±48 ppm, TESS-SPOC p_constant 4.372e-09 depth 144±40 ppm (sectors 57 -54±62, 84 65±72 ppm)

reasons.why: Machine-learned scorer ranks this as less planet-like than ~82% of known planets, consistent with the strong odd/even and secondary/ variability evidence for a false positive.
